index.title: MapleSteps: free guide for newcomers to Canada
index.desc: Free, plain-language guide for newcomers and immigrants to Canada: first steps, housing, jobs, health care, banking and taxes.
index.h1: Your first months in Canada, one step at a time
index.lead: Plain-language guides for newcomers and immigrants. Free, independent, and linked to official sources.
index.guides_lead: Start with the checklist, then read what you need now.
numbers: Police, fire or ambulance. Free from any phone.
Food, housing, settlement and other local services.
Talk to a nurse in most provinces. Not for emergencies.
index.free_h: Free settlement help is near you
index.free_p: Government-funded organizations across Canada help newcomers find housing, jobs, language classes and schools. Many have staff who speak your language, and most services are free for permanent residents and refugees.

first-steps.card: A checklist for your first weeks, in the right order.
first-steps.title: First steps in Canada: newcomer checklist
first-steps.desc: A step-by-step checklist for your first weeks in Canada: SIN, health card, bank account, phone, settlement services and benefits.
first-steps.lead: Tick off each step as you go. Most can be done in your first two weeks, and settlement workers can help with any of them for free.
checklist: Store your passport, Confirmation of Permanent Residence or permit, and landing papers somewhere safe. Keep copies and photos.
Apply for your Social Insurance Number (SIN)
You need a SIN to work and to get government benefits. Apply online or at a Service Canada office. It is free.
Apply for your provincial health card
Apply as soon as you arrive. Some provinces have a waiting period, so buy private insurance to cover it.
Bring your passport and immigration document. Ask about newcomer accounts with no monthly fee.
Compare prepaid and monthly plans. A local number helps with job applications and appointments.
They help with housing, jobs, forms and language classes, usually for free.
Public school is free. Contact your local school board with your children's documents.
Newcomers can apply to the Canada Revenue Agency for payments like the Canada child benefit and the GST/HST credit.
Each province has its own rules for exchanging a foreign licence. Some countries' licences can be exchanged directly.
Eligible newcomers can take free English or French classes. Ask your settlement agency.

items: Keep a folder with copies of every form you send and every letter you get.
Government agencies never ask for payment by gift card, crypto or wire transfer.
When you move, update your address with IRCC, your bank and the CRA.

housing.card: Where to look, what landlords ask for, and how to avoid scams.
housing.title: Renting a home in Canada: guide for newcomers
housing.desc: How newcomers can find a place to rent in Canada, what landlords ask for, tenant rights and how to avoid rental scams.
housing.lead: Most newcomers start by renting. Prices and rules depend on your city and province, so plan early and ask for help.

items: Online rental listings and local community groups
Your settlement agency, which may know newcomer-friendly landlords
Short-term rentals or temporary housing while you search
Rooms in shared homes, which cost less in expensive cities
A rental application with your income or job offer
References from past landlords or employers
A credit check. With no Canadian credit yet, offer bank statements as proof you can pay
A deposit. What a landlord can legally ask for depends on your province
Ask for a written lease and read it before you sign
Each province has its own tenant rules and an office that settles disputes
A landlord cannot refuse you because of your race, religion, country of origin or family status
Keep a receipt for every payment
Never send money before you see the place and meet the landlord
Be careful when the rent is much lower than similar homes nearby
Don't share your passport or SIN until you have signed a lease
Pay in a way that leaves a record, never by gift card or crypto

work.card: Job search, Canadian-style résumés and licensed professions.
work.title: Finding work in Canada: guide for newcomers
work.desc: How newcomers can find a job in Canada: official job boards, Canadian-style résumés, licensed professions and your rights at work.
work.lead: A first Canadian job often comes through people you meet. Use official job boards, free employment programs and every connection you have.

items: Job Bank, the Government of Canada's free job board
Free employment programs at settlement agencies, including mentoring and job fairs
Networking: tell friends, neighbours and community groups what work you want
Volunteering, which builds Canadian experience and references
Keep it to one or two pages
Leave out your photo, age, marital status and religion
Show results with numbers where you can
Write a short cover letter for each job
Doctors, nurses, engineers, teachers and many trades need a licence from a provincial regulator
Start the licensing process early, even before you arrive
You may need your education assessed
While you work toward your licence, look for related jobs in your field
Each province sets its own minimum wage and work rules
You should get a pay stub that shows your hours and deductions
You can refuse work that is unsafe
An employer cannot make you pay to get a job

health.card: Get your health card, find a doctor and know what is covered.
health.title: Health care in Canada: guide for newcomers
health.desc: How health care works for newcomers to Canada: provincial health cards, waiting periods, what is covered and how to find a doctor.
health.lead: Each province and territory runs its own public health insurance plan. Apply for your card as soon as you arrive.

items: Apply to your province or territory's health plan right after you arrive
Some provinces have a waiting period of up to three months
Buy private insurance to cover any waiting period
Resettled refugees and refugee claimants may get temporary coverage from the federal government
Medically necessary doctor visits and hospital care
Usually not covered for most adults: dental care, glasses and many prescriptions
Employer benefit plans often cover these extras
Some provinces have programs for children, seniors and low-income families
Register for a family doctor. Many areas have a waiting list
Use walk-in clinics while you wait
Call 811 in most provinces to speak with a nurse
Call 911 or go to an emergency room in an emergency
Moving to a new country is stressful. Asking for help is normal
Call or text 988 at any time if you are thinking about suicide
Settlement agencies can connect you with counsellors who speak your language

money.card: Banking, building credit, taxes and benefits.
money.title: Banking, credit and taxes for newcomers to Canada
money.desc: A newcomer's guide to banking in Canada, building a credit history, filing taxes, getting benefits and avoiding scams.
money.lead: A few early steps make life much easier: a bank account, a credit history, and filing your taxes every year.

items: Most banks offer newcomer accounts with lower fees in the first year
A chequing account is for daily spending; a savings account is for saving
Compare monthly fees and transaction limits before you choose
Your credit history starts at zero in Canada
A secured credit card is an easy way to start
Pay the full balance on time every month
Check your credit report for free with Equifax and TransUnion
File a tax return every year, even with no income, to keep getting benefits
The deadline for most people is April 30
In your first year, you can apply for benefits before you file
Free tax clinics can file a simple return for you
The CRA never asks for payment by gift card, crypto or e-transfer to a person
Hang up on calls that threaten arrest or deportation
When in doubt, call the CRA using the number on its official website

about.title: About MapleSteps | MapleSteps
about.desc: Who runs MapleSteps, how the site is funded, and how we handle your privacy.
about.lead: MapleSteps is a free, independent guide for newcomers to Canada, written in plain language and available in six languages.

sections.p: We are an independent website. We are not part of the Government of Canada or any immigration agency, and we do not give legal or immigration advice. For your own situation, contact a settlement agency or an authorized professional.

MapleSteps is free because of advertising. Some pages may include affiliate links. If you buy through one, we may earn a small commission at no extra cost to you. We only recommend things we believe help newcomers.
Found a mistake or have a suggestion? Email hello@maplesteps.ca.

privacy.title: Privacy Policy | MapleSteps
privacy.desc: How MapleSteps handles your information, cookies and advertising, including Google AdSense, and how to opt out of personalized ads.
privacy.lead: Last updated: November 7, 2026. This policy explains what information is collected when you visit maplesteps.ca and how it is used.

sections.p: MapleSteps (maplesteps.ca) is an independent website that publishes free guides for newcomers to Canada. It is not a government website.
You can use MapleSteps without creating an account or giving us any personal information. If you email us, we receive your email address and your message, and we use them only to reply to you.

Ticks on the first-steps checklist and your language choice are saved only in your own browser (local storage). They are not sent to us. You can clear them at any time with the "Clear my checklist" button or in your browser settings.

MapleSteps is free because it shows ads. Third-party vendors, including Google, use cookies to serve ads based on your prior visits to this website or other websites. Google's use of advertising cookies enables it and its partners to serve ads to you based on your visits to this site and/or other sites on the internet.

sections.h: How to opt out of personalized ads
sections.p: You can turn off personalized advertising in Google's Ads Settings. You can also opt out of other vendors' use of cookies for personalized advertising at youradchoices.ca (Canada) or aboutads.info. In some regions, including the European Economic Area and the United Kingdom, you will be asked for your consent before personalized ads are shown.

The site is hosted by Cloudflare, which processes basic technical data, such as IP addresses, to deliver pages and protect the site from attacks. We may use privacy-friendly statistics to count visits. We do not sell personal information.
Our guides link to government and other websites. Those sites have their own privacy policies, which we encourage you to read.
MapleSteps is written for adults. We do not knowingly collect personal information from children.
We may update this policy from time to time. The date at the top shows the latest version. If you have questions about your privacy, email hello@maplesteps.ca.
